notes.meaning: The struggle between the families of Saul and David dragged on for years, mostly through occasional skirmishes rather than massive battles. David's position grew steadily stronger as more people recognized God's hand on him, while Saul's dynasty steadily declined. God's promises often unfold over time, teaching His people patience as they wait on Him.

During his years in Hebron, David began having sons, starting with his firstborn, Amnon, by his wife Ahinoam. A growing family was an ancient sign of an expanding and stable royal house, though Amnon's life would later bring great sorrow.

David's second son was Chileab (also called Daniel), and his third was Absalom. Absalom's mother was Maacah, a foreign princess from Geshur in Syria, whom David likely married to secure a northern political alliance.

David had three more sons in Hebron: Adonijah, Shephatiah, and Ithream, each born to a different wife. Although having many wives and children made David look powerful to surrounding nations, taking multiple wives ignored God's law and planted seeds of future family heartbreak.
As the war continued, Saul's general Abner strengthened his personal control over the northern tribes. He made himself the real authority and driving force behind Saul's weak son Ish-bosheth.

Ish-bosheth challenged Abner for sleeping with Rizpah, who had been a concubine (a secondary wife) of King Saul. In the ancient world, taking a deceased king's concubine was often viewed as a move to seize the royal throne.

Abner reacted with fierce anger, asking if Ish-bosheth viewed him as nothing more than a worthless, traitorous dog from Judah. He reminded the king that his loyalty and military strength were the only reasons Saul's family had not already fallen to David.

Abner took a solemn oath that he would take the kingdom away from Saul's family and place David on the throne over all Israel and Judah. His statement revealed that he had known God's plan all along, yet had opposed it until his own pride was offended.
Ish-bosheth was so terrified of Abner that he could not utter a single word in reply. His helpless silence exposed how completely he depended on his general to stay in power.

Abner sent envoys to David to propose a covenant, offering to deliver the allegiance of all the northern tribes. He spoke with great pride, acting as though the fate of the entire land rested in his own hands.

David agreed to enter into a peace agreement, but demanded one essential condition: Abner must bring Saul's daughter Michal back to him. Michal was David's first lawful wife, and having her back would also strengthen his claim to Saul's throne.

David formally asked Ish-bosheth to return Michal, reminding him that he had legally won her by killing one hundred Philistine enemies as her bride-price. Making this official request forced Ish-bosheth to acknowledge David's rights and show his own inability to refuse.

Ish-bosheth took Michal away from her second husband, Paltiel, who wept openly as he followed her until Abner ordered him to turn back. While Paltiel's grief was real, Michal was David's rightful wife who had been unlawfully taken from him by Saul years earlier.

Abner met with the tribal leaders of Israel, reminding them that they had wanted David as king in the past. He urged them to act immediately because the Lord had appointed David to save Israel from the Philistines and their other enemies.

Abner held private talks with the tribe of Benjamin because they were Saul's kinsmen and stood to lose royal standing if the kingship left their tribe. After convincing them, Abner went to Hebron to inform David that both Benjamin and the rest of Israel were ready to follow him.

When Abner arrived in Hebron with twenty representative leaders, David hosted a covenant meal to seal their new friendship. Abner promised to gather all Israel to make a formal national treaty with David, and David sent him away in peace.

Right after Abner left, Joab and David's men returned from a successful raid carrying great spoil. When Joab arrived, his officers told him that Abner had met with the king and had been allowed to depart peacefully.

Joab confronted David with harsh words, asking why he had let Abner go instead of arresting him. He claimed Abner had come only as a spy to gather military intelligence, disguising his own personal jealousy behind concern for the king.
Without David's knowledge, Joab sent messengers to fetch Abner back from the well of Sirah. Abner had complete confidence in David's promise of peace, so he returned without suspecting any trap.

When Abner reached the city gate of Hebron, Joab pulled him aside as if to share a private word and stabbed him to death. Joab claimed he was avenging his brother Asahel, but he was also secretly getting rid of a gifted military rival.

When David heard what had happened, he declared before the Lord that he and his throne were entirely innocent of Abner's death. He wanted all Israel to know that he had neither ordered nor approved of this murder.

David called down a severe curse on Joab and his family, praying that they would suffer from disease, physical weakness, violence, and poverty. David was outraged because Joab's attack was an act of cold-blooded murder committed in a city of refuge.

Joab and his brother Abishai were both guilty of the murder because they planned it together in revenge for their brother Asahel. Yet their revenge was unlawful, since Abner had killed Asahel during open battle in self-defense, not by treachery.

David ordered Joab and all the people to tear their clothes and put on rough sackcloth to mourn publicly for Abner. The king himself walked behind the funeral frame as the chief mourner, showing his deep sorrow and forcing Joab to take part in public shame.

They buried Abner in Hebron, and David wept loudly at the gravesite while all the people joined in his tears. Burying Abner in David's own capital city honored the fallen leader and showed the northern tribes that David genuinely grieved for him.

David sang a lament asking if Abner had died like a senseless fool or a condemned criminal. He pointed out that Abner was a brave warrior who was never captured or bound in chains, but was instead brought down by the underhanded trickery of wicked men.

The people urged David to eat food during the day, which was customary after a funeral, but David swore an oath to fast until sunset. His refusal to eat proved to everyone that his grief was heartfelt and not just an empty show.

The people observed David's humble behavior and fasting, and they were well pleased with everything the king did. On that day, all his troops and the people of Israel were fully convinced that David had no role in Abner's death.
David told his officers that a great prince and mighty commander had fallen that day in Israel. He wanted his court to understand the heavy loss the nation had suffered through Abner's death.

David confessed that his newly established reign was still tender and vulnerable, and that his nephews Joab and Abishai were too powerful for him to punish directly. Rather than risking a civil uprising, he trusted the Lord to bring justice upon the wrongdoer in His own time.
